'''''Zinnia elegans''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Zinnia violacea'') known as '''youth-and-age''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''common zinnia''' or '''elegant zinnia''', is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[flowering plant]] in the [[family (botany)|family]] [[Asteraceae]]. It is [[native species|native]] to Mexico but grown as an ornamental in many places and naturalised in several places, including scattered locations in South and Central America, the West Indies, the United States, Australia, and Italy.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Zinnia%20elegans.png|title=Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map|website=bonap.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=zinnia+elegans|title=''Zinnia elegans'' Jacq.|website=Flora Italiana}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://bie.ala.org.au/species/Zinnia+elegans|title=Zinnia elegans : Zinnia – Atlas of Living Australia|first=Atlas of Living|last=Australia|website=bie.ala.org.au}}</ref><ref>Berendsohn, W.G. & A.E. Cuscatlania 1(3): 290–1–290–13</ref><ref>Dodson, C.H., A.H. Gentry & F.M. Valverde Badillo. (1985). ''La Flora de Jauneche: Los Ríos, Ecuador''. ==Description==
The uncultivated plant grows to about {{convert|5.27|in|cm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} in height. It has solitary flower heads about {{convert|2|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on}} across. The purple ray  florets surround black and yellow discs. The [[lanceolate]] leaves are opposite the flower heads. Flowering occurs during the summer months.

==History==
The species was first collected in 1789 at [[Tixtla]], [[Guerrero]], by [[Martín Sessé y Lacasta|Sessé]] and [[José Mariano Mociño|Mociño]]. It was formally described as ''Zinnia violacea'' by [[Antonio José Cavanilles|Cavanilles]] in 1791. [[Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin|Jacquin]] described it again in 1792 as ''Zinnia elegans'', which was the name that Sessé and Moçiño had used in their manuscript of ''Plantae Novae Hispaniae'', which was not published until 1890.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Kirkbride, J. H. |author2= Wiersma, J. H.|year=2007|title= Proposal to conserve the name ''Zinnia elegans'' against ''Z. violacea''|doi=10.2307/25065881 |doi-access=free |journal=Taxon|volume= 56|issue=3|pages=958–959|jstor= 25065881}}</ref> The genus was named by [[Carl von Linné]] after the German botanist [[Johann Gottfried Zinn]], who described the species now known as ''[[Zinnia peruviana]]'' in 1757 as ''Rudbeckia foliis oppositis hirsutis ovato-acutis, calyce imbricatus, radii petalis pistillatis''. Linné realised that it was not a ''[[Rudbeckia]]''.

==Cultivation==
The garden zinnia was bred via [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridisation]] from the wild form. Zinnias are popular garden plants with hundreds of [[cultivars]] in many flower colours, sizes and forms. There are giant forms with flower heads up to {{cvt|15|cm|in|0}} in diameter.

Flower colours range from white and cream to pinks, reds, and purples, to green, yellow, [[apricot (colour)|apricot]], orange, [[salmon (colour)|salmon]], and bronze. Some are striped, speckled or bicoloured. There are "[[pom-pom]]" forms that resemble [[dahlias]]. Sizes range from dwarf varieties of less than {{cvt|15|cm|in|0}} in height to {{cvt|90|cm|ft|0}} tall. The [[powdery mildew]] common to zinnias in humid climates is less common in recently developed varieties, which are resistant.

Other cultivars include 'Magellan', 'Envy Double', 'Fireworks', 'Blue Point Purple', 'Profusion Cherry', 'Profusion Orange', 'Star Gold', 'Star Orange', and several white-flowered types such as 'Crystal White', 'Purity', and 'Profusion White'. Mixed-colour seed selections are available.

===Growth===
Zinnias grow easily and prefer well-drained, [[loam]]y soil and full sun. They grow best in dry, warm, frost-free regions, and many kinds are drought-tolerant. As they do not tolerate freezing temperatures, in [[temperate climate|temperate]] zones they must be sown after all danger of frost has passed. Alternatively, they may be sown under cover and carefully transplanted into their final positions when the soil warms up.
